videos.title: The Charge That Destroyed Britain's Army in Ten Minutes
videos.desc:
October 5, 1813. A bugle sounds over a swampy stretch of Upper Canada, and one thousand Kentucky horsemen charge straight into the British 41st Regiment of Foot. Within five minutes, 601 redcoats have surrendered, the cannon never fires a shot, and the general is already riding for the rear.

This is the story of the Battle of the Thames, the clash that ended British control of the western frontier and cost Tecumseh his life.

In this video, we cover:

• How Tecumseh built a Native confederacy stretching from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast
• The Brock and Tecumseh partnership that took Fort

videos.title: How One American Ship Outran Britain's Entire Squadron
videos.desc:
In the summer of 1812, the United States had sixteen warships. Britain had over six hundred. And yet one American frigate outran five British warships in a sixty-hour chase across the open Atlantic, then came back a month later and sent HMS Guerriere to the bottom.

This is the story of the USS Constitution, the ship that earned the name Old Ironsides.

Inside this video:

• How shipbuilder Joshua Humphreys designed a frigate to break the rules, with live oak hulls twenty-two inches thick
• Captain Isaac Hull's desperate escape using kedging anchors, wet sails, and a well-timed rain squall

videos.title: The Disguise That Destroyed Britain's Loyalist Army
videos.desc:
February 1781. A Continental cavalry officer rides straight into the middle of an enemy column, shakes the commander's hand, and watches a friendly greeting turn into one of the bloodiest ambushes of the American Revolution.

Henry "Light Horse Harry" Lee wore a green coat that looked almost identical to the one worn by Banastre Tarleton's British Legion. Three hundred North Carolina Loyalists, marching to join Cornwallis, mistook him for the very man they were hoping to meet. What followed lasted only minutes, yet it helped unravel the British Southern strategy.

videos.title: The Fake Campfires That Fooled Britain's Army
videos.desc:
The night of January 2, 1777: Lord Cornwallis had George Washington pinned against Assunpink Creek, with the Delaware River at his back and every escape route covered. He went to bed planning to "bag the fox" in the morning.

By dawn, the fox was gone.

In this video, Ravelin breaks down how Washington used smoldering campfires, rag-wrapped wagon wheels, and a road that froze solid just in time to slip a 5,000-man army around the largest British force in America. The story takes in the collapse of the Continental Army in late 1776, the Christmas crossing of the Delaware, the desperate defense

The Christmas Night Crossing Of The Delaware

videos.title: The 28-Day Siege That Drove Britain Out of the South
videos.desc:
Fifty men charged the Star Fort at Ninety Six. Thirty became casualties in under an hour. Nathanael Greene failed to take the fort… and still helped force the British out of the Southern interior anyway.

In this episode, we break down the 1781 Siege of Ninety Six, one of the most overlooked battles of the American Revolution. From Greene’s strategy of survival and attrition to Kosciuszko’s trenches, mine tunnel, and siege tower, to John Harris Cruger’s fierce Loyalist defense of the Star Fort, this is the story of a battle the Americans lost—and a campaign that still helped win the war.

videos.title: The Ambush That Taught Washington How to Beat Britain
videos.desc:
How did George Washington survive Braddock’s Defeat when hundreds around him fell? On July 9, 1755, a sick 23-year-old Washington rode into the Pennsylvania wilderness and emerged from one of the British Army’s worst disasters with four bullet holes in his coat and two horses shot from under him.

This video follows the Battle of the Monongahela, the collapse of General Edward Braddock’s expedition, and the brutal lessons Washington carried with him into the American Revolution. videos.title: How a Starving Army Came Back to Humiliate Britain
videos.desc:
❄️ Valley Forge was supposed to be the end of the American Revolution.

Starving, shoeless, and ravaged by disease, Washington’s army entered the winter of 1777 in ruins. With Philadelphia in British hands and Congress on the run, few believed the Continental Army would survive to see spring. But inside that frozen camp, something extraordinary happened: suffering forged discipline, chaos gave way to order, and a broken force became a real army.
